summary: Specifies how defect states are mapped between Ethernet attachment circuits and the Ethernet pseudowires linked to them, so an end-to-end emulated Ethernet service can report failures consistently. It standardizes how provider edge routers react to defects on either side.

eli5.summary: If a road is broken, signs must tell the next town. This says how network boxes pass the news of a broken link along.

questions: pe behavior on ethernet pw defects
what is a pseudowire defect state
subtitle: Spells out how provider edge routers pass failure news between Ethernet links and the pseudowires that carry them.

tldr.problem: RFC 6310 maps defect states between pseudowires and attachment circuits but does not cover Ethernet, so routers could differ in which alarms they raise and what they do about a failure.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines entry and exit criteria for four defect states (AC receive, AC transmit, PW receive, PW transmit) and the Ethernet OAM and pseudowire notifications a provider edge MUST send when each state starts or ends.
tldr.outcome: Failures on either side of an emulated Ethernet service are reported to the other side in an unambiguous way.

today: RFC 7023 is a Proposed Standard (October 2013). The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it builds on RFC 6310.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6310 specifies how defect states are mapped and signaled between a pseudowire (PW) and the attachment circuit (AC) of an emulated service, for technologies such as ATM and Frame Relay. It does not describe this for the Ethernet PW service because of Ethernet's unique characteristics.

RFC 7023 fills that gap for ACs and Ethernet PWs built under the PWE3 architecture (RFC 3985). As in RFC 6310, the aim is to standardize how provider edge (PE) routers behave on failures, so there is no ambiguity about the alarms generated and the actions taken.
sections.eli5: An older rulebook told network boxes how to pass along news of broken links for some kinds of traffic, but not Ethernet. This memo adds the Ethernet rules.

sections.title: Overview of the Ethernet OAM Pieces
sections.content:
The RFC covers these Ethernet OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) mechanisms and how they interwork with PW OAM: Ethernet Link OAM, the Ethernet Local Management Interface (E-LMI), Ethernet Continuity Check (CC) and Alarm Indication Signal (AIS) with Remote Defect Indication (RDI). CFM and Y.1731 mechanisms apply to all types of Ethernet ACs, while Link OAM and E-LMI are optional.

Native service OAM can simply ride across the PW as user data. For example, continuity check messages (CCMs) between two MEPs can be carried this way, and a service failure is detected when CCMs are not received for 3.5 times the local CCM transmission interval. That is not always enough: a PE may need to identify which domain failed, scaling may rule out running CCMs, and a PE may be unable to process native OAM messages arriving on the PW. So alarms generated in one domain must be mapped into the other.

In multi-segment PWs, switching PEs are not aware of the native service, so they rely on PW OAM. Mapping to native OAM is then needed at the terminating PEs.
sections.eli5: Some failures can be spotted just by noticing that regular check-in messages stopped. But the boxes in the middle may not understand those messages, so they need their own way to pass along the bad news.

sections.title: The Four Defect States
sections.content:
Seen from PE1, with CE1 on its attachment circuit and PE2 across the PW, there are four abstract defect states, using the conventions of RFC 6310. Each names the direction of user traffic that is affected.

  • PW receive defect: PE1 cannot receive traffic on the PW.
  • PW transmit defect: PE1 cannot send user traffic toward CE2. PE1 may learn this through a Reverse Defect Indication from PE2.
  • AC receive defect: PE1 cannot receive user traffic from CE1 over the AC.
  • AC transmit defect: PE1 cannot send user traffic on the local AC.

If both a receive and a transmit defect are identified at once, the receive defect state SHOULD take precedence in handling.
sections.eli5: A box can have trouble hearing from the pipe, talking into the pipe, hearing from the customer, or talking to the customer. Those are the four kinds of trouble.

sections.title: PW Status and How PW Defects Are Signaled
sections.content:
All the PW defects of RFC 6310 apply to Ethernet PWs, and any of its detection mechanisms can be used. For PWs set up with LDP, the default way to signal AC and PW status is the LDP status notification message (RFC 4447). For PWs set up another way, such as static configuration, in-band VCCV-BFD (RFC 5885) SHOULD be used, or alternatively the mechanisms of RFC 6478 MAY be used.

Two status code points matter. A forward defect is a logical OR of local AC receive fault, local PW transmit fault and PW not forwarding. A reverse defect is a logical OR of local AC transmit fault and local PW receive fault.

When VCCV is used, the CV type decides how defects travel. With CV type 0x04 or 0x10, BFD detects only PW faults and other defects go through LDP status messages. With CV type 0x08 or 0x20, BFD is used for both detection and AC/PW fault notification, so all defects are signaled via BFD.

A PE using native service OAM can also notify its peer by sending AIS frames, suspending CCM frames, or setting the RDI bit in transmitted CCM frames, and it undoes these when the defect clears.
sections.eli5: There are a few different ways to send the warning message, and which one is used depends on how the connection was set up.

sections.title: When an Ethernet AC Enters or Leaves a Defect State
sections.content:
PE1 enters the AC receive defect state if it sees a physical-layer fault (for example loss of signal, a Link OAM critical event with Dying Gasp or Critical Event, or a client Signal Fail), if a MEP on the AC receives an AIS frame from CE1, if no CCMs arrive from the peer MEP within 3.5 times the configured CCM period, or if a CCM carries an Interface Status TLV saying interface down. A CCM with the wrong MEG ID, MEP ID or MEP level SHOULD be treated as an AC receive defect. PE1 leaves the state when all of these causes are cleared.

PE1 enters the AC transmit defect state on a physical-layer fault such as a Link OAM Link Fault indication, or when a MEP with CCM transmission enabled receives a CCM from CE1 with the RDI bit set. It leaves when those conditions clear.
sections.eli5: A box decides its link to the customer is bad if the signal vanishes, a warning arrives, or the regular check-in notes stop coming. It decides it is fine when all of those go away.

sections.title: Interworking Procedures
sections.content:
For each of the four states, the RFC says what PE1 MUST do when the state starts and when it ends. The general idea: a defect on the PW side is relayed to CE1 through Ethernet OAM, and a defect on the AC side is relayed to PE2 through PW signaling.

On PW receive defect entry, a PE with a Down MEP on the AC transmits AIS frames if CCM transmission is off. If CCMs are on, it sends CCMs with the Interface Status TLV as Down when the MEP supports that TLV, and otherwise stops sending CCMs. If E-LMI is used, it sends an asynchronous STATUS message saying the PW is Not Active. If PE1 found the defect itself, it MUST also send PE2 a reverse defect notification. On exit it reverses each action, for example by sending Interface Status Up and an E-LMI message saying the PW is Active.

On PW transmit defect entry, the MEP sets the RDI bit in CCMs or sends an Interface Status of down, E-LMI reports Not Active, and if PE1 detected the failure without a reverse defect notification from PE2 it MUST send PE2 a forward defect indication (FDI). On exit, the RDI bit is cleared, E-LMI reports Active and the FDI is cleared.

On AC receive defect entry, PE1 MUST send PE2 a forward defect notification, and a Down MEP with CCMs enabled MUST set the RDI bit. On AC transmit defect entry, PE1 MUST send PE2 a reverse defect notification. Exit procedures clear these notifications.
sections.eli5: The rule is simple: bad news from the pipe is passed to the customer, and bad news from the customer side is passed down the pipe. When it is fixed, the all-clear goes the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The interworking mechanisms do not change the security functions of the messages themselves. The generic PW security considerations of RFC 3985 apply to native OAM messages carried inside the PW, the VCCV considerations of RFC 5085 apply to those messages, and the PWE3 control protocol considerations of RFC 4447 apply to indications carried in LDP status messages.

Because fault conditions propagate between native service networks and the packet switched network, end-to-end service continuity depends on a trust relationship between the operators of those networks.
sections.eli5: Passing warnings between two networks only works if the people running them trust each other. The usual safety rules for these messages still apply.

sections.title: Background on Ethernet OAM
sections.content:
The informative appendix explains that Ethernet OAM covers Fault Management and Performance Monitoring. Y.1731 covers both, while IEEE CFM covers a subset of fault management. A Maintenance Entity is a point-to-point association, and a Maintenance Entity Group (MEG) groups several. MEPs originate OAM frames, and MIPs between them respond to those frames without originating them. Up to 8 MEG levels allow end-to-end and segment monitoring at the same time.

The fault management tools common to CFM and Y.1731 are Continuity Check Messages, Loopback Messages and Replies, and Link Trace Messages and Replies. Y.1731 adds AIS, plus performance tools for loss and delay measurement.
sections.eli5: Ethernet has its own toolbox for checking that links work and for measuring how well they do. This part lists the tools.
